tip: Sympa is the everyday clip of sympathique – both mean nice or friendly. It still adds -s in the plural: 'des voisins sympas'.
Marron never adds -e or -s: it's really the word for chestnut, so 'les chaussures marron' stays flat even in the plural.
French has no apostrophe-s. 'My neighbor's garden' becomes 'le jardin de mon voisin' – literally 'the garden of my neighbor'.
Weather takes 'il fait', not 'il est': 'il fait froid' means it's cold. 'Il est froid' would be about a person being cold.
The easiest question needs no extra words: keep normal order and raise your voice. 'Ça te plaît ici ?' is a statement asked with a rising tone.
The feminine ending wakes up a silent letter: masculine 'brun' ends silently, but 'brune' sounds the n.
The feminine -e makes the final consonant audible: masculine 'petit' ends silently, 'petite' sounds the t.
21 and its cousins take a bare 'et', no hyphens: 'vingt et un', trente et un. But most compounds just hyphenate: vingt-deux, trente-trois.
The feminine adds a grave accent: masculine 'fier' becomes 'fière', the same spelling shift as premier/première.
Sortir uses être, not avoir, in the past: 'il est sorti' = he went out. Never 'il a sorti' for going out.
Rester takes être even though nobody moves: 'nous sommes restés' = we stayed. Staying put still counts as an être verb.
The tu command drops the -s: you write 'tu regardes' but 'Regarde !' when telling someone to look.
French literally says 'I raise myself': 'je me lève' = I get up. Drop the 'me' and 'je lève' just means I lift something else.
'à + le' must merge into 'au': you can't say 'à le restaurant', only 'au restaurant'.
'le' shrinks to l' before a vowel: 'le après-midi' becomes 'l'après-midi', the e dropped and joined on.
Two past tenses in one breath: 'connaissais' is the ongoing state (already knew), 'a posé' the single action that happened.
To say what day it is, French uses 'we are': 'nous sommes lundi' = it's Monday, literally 'we are Monday'.
Like English 'going to', French uses aller + verb for the near future: 'je vais ... partir' = I'm going to leave.
'Il y a' means 'there is', not 'he has' (that's 'il a'). The y is mandatory: 'il y a du soleil' = it's sunny.
Dates use plain numbers where English counts 'fifteenth': 'le quinze mars'. Only the 1st is ordinal – le premier.
'En fait' means 'actually, in fact'. Don't reach for the false friend 'actuellement' – that one means 'currently'.
The imparfait sets the scene, the passé composé breaks it: 'dînaient' was the ongoing dinner, 's'est éteinte' the sudden moment the light died.
'Voulais' is the ongoing wish (I wanted to), 'a fermé' the one event that killed it – passé composé for what suddenly happened.
With être the participle agrees in writing only: 'est montée' adds an -e for she, but it sounds exactly like 'monté'.
Être builds its own past with avoir, not itself: 'il a été malade' = he was sick. Never 'il est été'.
French 'makes' attention rather than paying it: 'faire attention' = to pay attention or to be careful.
'Il y avait' is simply the past of 'il y a' (there is): 'il y avait du monde' = there were people. One fixed phrase, not a verb to conjugate.
Passer flips helpers by meaning: être for moving through ('nous sommes passés par...'), but avoir for spending time – j'ai passé une semaine.
'Ils sont morts' looks like 'they are dead' but it's the past of mourir: 'they died'. Mourir takes être.
'À cette époque' (back then) is a cue for the imparfait: 'travaillait' paints how life was, not a single finished event.
'Ils devaient' = they were supposed to, leaving it open whether they did. 'Ils ont dû' would mean they had to and actually did.
Verbs of movement like aller take être, not avoir: 'nous sommes allés' = we went. Most other verbs use avoir.
English 'had been raining' is just imparfait + depuis in French: 'il pleuvait depuis deux heures' = it had been raining for two hours.
'Avoir envie de' means to feel like, not to envy: 'j'ai eu envie de partir' = I felt like leaving. French 'has' the urge.
'Avoir l'habitude de' = to be used to, literally 'to have the habit of': 'nous avions l'habitude de dîner' = we usually had dinner.
'Il pouvait courir' = he was able to, a standing ability. Switch to 'il a pu' and it means he managed to, that one time.
Feelings live in the imparfait: 'avais faim' (were hungry) is the ongoing state, 'es rentré' (came home) the completed action framing it.
Age in the past is always imparfait: 'tu avais dix ans' = you were ten. The move, 'as déménagé', is the one-off event.
No -e on 'coupé' here: in 'elle s'est coupé le doigt' the finger is the real object, so the participle doesn't agree with elle.
'Se tromper de' + noun = to get the wrong one: 'je me suis trompé de route' = I took the wrong road.
The imparfait is the backdrop, the passé composé the event: 'il pleuvait' (was raining) when 'nous sommes sortis' (we went out).
Remembering is reflexive in French and drags 'de' along: 'tu te souviens de...' = do you remember...? Literally 'you remind yourself of'.
'Il faut que' forces the subjunctive: it's 'prenne', not 'prend'. Necessity plus que changes the verb's form.
'Qui ait', not 'qui a': the hotel isn't real yet, you're still searching for one. Wanting something uncertain triggers the subjunctive.
After 'il faut que', être turns into 'soit': 'que tout le monde soit prêt', never 'est'. One of the most irregular subjunctives.
The object pronoun tucks inside the ne...pas wrapper: 'je ne le sais pas'. 'Le' stays glued to the verb, not after 'pas'.
